steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Socialisation is the process through which individuals learn the norms, values and culture of their society. Primary socialisation (0-5 years): family teaches basic norms, language, and values. Secondary socialisation (5+ years): school, peers, media and religion reinforce and extend social learning.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Norms are social rules that guide behaviour (e.g. queuing, shaking hands). Values are broad beliefs about what is good and desirable (e.g. democracy, equality, achievement). Norms are specific; values are general. Norms enforce values through sanctions (positive: praise; negative: disapproval).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Status: a social position within a group. Ascribed status: given at birth (gender, ethnicity, royal family). Achieved status: earned through effort (qualifications, career). Role: the behaviour expected of someone with a particular status (teachers are expected to teach, mark work, and maintain discipline).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Culture: the way of life of a particular society, including norms, values, language, beliefs and material objects. Subculture: a smaller group within society with distinct norms and values (e.g. youth subcultures, religious groups). Cultural diversity: different cultures coexisting within one society.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between primary and secondary socialisation, with examples. | Describe the relationship between norms, values and sanctions. | Evaluate whether socialisation determines our identity or whether we have free choice.

steps.body: Primary socialisation: family teaches basic norms (saying please/thank you), language, right/wrong, and core values (honesty, respect). steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Primary = family (0-5). Secondary = school, peers, media (5+). Both shape identity. Values = broad beliefs. Norms = specific rules. Sanctions = rewards/punishments that enforce norms. Ascribed status = given (birth). Achieved status = earned (effort). Modern societies value achieved status.
